Dear Dr. Oz: 
The undersigned national organizations, representing digestive disease patients and physicians 
appreciate the opportunity to respond to several elements of the Centers for Medicare & 
Medicaid Services (CMS) proposed rule, as published in the Federal Register on April 14, 2026, 
to improve the electronic exchange of health care data and streamline processes related to prior 
authorization (PA) by increasing the interoperability of systems used across the health care 
industry.  
The use of PA is resulting in denials and delays for medically necessary care and treatments, and 
the administrative burden associated with PA on gastroenterologists and other physicians, as well 
as the impact of PA on clinical recommendations, are well documented. , ,   We acknowledge the

PA process more transparent. The truth is, however, that the PA data required to be made public 
by health plans are often difficult to find on health plan websites, reported in inconsistent 
formats, and aggregated at a level too high to show what is happening to specific services, such 
as diagnostic endoscopy or advanced therapeutic procedures. High approval rates on paper may 
also mask delays that effectively function as denials for patients with time-sensitive conditions. 
Greater transparency is required and is why our societies strongly advocate for the reporting by 
health plans of PA metrics at a granular level, including approvals and denials by service and 
item category, as well as the number of requests denied and appealed using AI or similar 
technology.

ELECTRONIC PA FOR ALL DRUGS THAT REQUIRE PA 
Our societies strongly support CMSâ€™ proposal to expand the 2024 interoperability and PA 
framework to include drugs, both those covered under a medical benefit and those covered under 
a pharmacy benefit, using a combination of standards, including the HL7Â® FHIRÂ® standards 
that compose the PA Application Programming Interface (API) and the National Council for 
Prescription Drug Programs (NCPDP) standards required for covered Part D drugs. 
PA requirements for medical- and pharmacy-benefit drugs are also among the most 
administratively burdensome utilization management practices faced by gastroenterology (GI) 
practices. Current processes remain highly fragmented and frequently rely on manual fax, 
telephone, or portal-based workflows that impede timely patient care. 
However, CMS could strengthen the proposal by: 
â€¢ Clarifying that all utilization management aspects related to drugs covered under a 
medical or pharmacy benefit, including site-of-care and dose escalation requests, be 
supported through the PA API and be included in transparency requirements.  
â€¢ Explicitly prohibiting payers from requiring clinicians to submit duplicative 
documentation through proprietary portals when equivalent information has already been 
transmitted through the standardized API. 
It is also critically important that there be some level of interoperability between medical 
and pharmacy benefit standards when establishing electronic PA for drugs.  It is common in 
IBD for therapies to cross the medical and pharmacy benefit categories. For example, a biologic 
may begin as IV induction under the medical benefit and later transition to subcutaneous 
maintenance under the pharmacy benefit. If pharmacy and medical benefit data are not 
interoperable, the payer may incorrectly view the patient as â€œnewâ€ to therapy or lacking 
documentation, even though the therapy is a continuation of established care. In addition, 
clinicians have all experienced situations in which IV induction is approved, only to have the 
subcutaneous maintenance denied. 
Response Timeframes 
Like non-drug medical items and services, impacted payers must be required to respond to PA 
requests for drugs in a timely manner. Delays associated with PA and step therapy are not merely 
administrative inconveniences but can result in clinically significant patient harm. Published 
literature shows that delays resulting from health plan utilization management tactics are often 
associated with increased disease activity, emergency department visits, hospitalizations and 
otherwise avoidable health care utilization. For patients with GI inflammatory conditions, 
delayed initiation of treatment or interruption in treatment can result in loss of response to 
treatment, immunogenicity, worsening disease and increased risk of surgery.   We support CMSâ€™

proposals to: 
â€¢ Require Qualified Health Plans (QHP) issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges 
(FFEs) to make PA decisions no later than 72 hours for standard requests and 24 hours 
for expedited requests for all drugs.  
â€¢ Require state Medicaid FFS programs, Medicaid managed care plans, and Childrenâ€™s 
Health Insurance Program (CHIP) managed care entities to make PA decisions for drugs 
within a timeframe that aligns with applicable existing decision timeframe requirements.  
â€¢ Require state CHIP Fee for Service (FFS) programs to make prior authorization 
decisions no later than 24 hours for prescription drugs for which Federal Financial 
Participation (FFP) is available. 
While our organizations support CMSâ€™ proposed timelines, we encourage the Agency to 
adopt the shortest feasible timelines across all payer categories. We recommend that all prior 
authorization requests involving liver transplant patients, including both transplant candidates 
and transplant recipients, be subject to expedited review within 24 hours regardless of stated 
acuity. Transplant patients frequently require urgent access to immunosuppressive therapies, anti-
infectives, and other specialty medications where delays can result in graft dysfunction, organ 
rejection, hospitalization, or other serious complications. Similarly, transplant candidates often 
require rapid treatment adjustments to preserve stability and maintain transplant eligibility. Given 
the uniquely time-sensitive nature of transplant care, a uniform expedited standard for transplant-
related prior authorizations is warranted. 
Patients with active GI disease often require urgent access to therapy to prevent irreversible 
complications. Delays in authorization can result in hospitalization, surgery, bowel damage, 
corticosteroid dependence, malnutrition, or disease progression. 
We further recommend that CMS: 
â€¢ Finalize the proposed expedited review timelines and strengthen enforcement 
mechanisms for noncompliance. 
â€¢ Require automatic approval when payers fail to meet applicable review deadlines. 
â€¢ Require continuity-of-care protections that maintain access to existing therapy during 
pending appeals or patient transitions between health plans.

PA USE TRANSPARENCY BY IMPACTED PAYERS 
Under the 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, impacted payers must 
report on their websites certain PA metrics for non-drug items and services by percentage, 
including the percentage of PAs that were approved, denied, approved after appeal, and approved 
after the timeframe for review was extended. We strongly support CMSâ€™ proposal to require 
impacted payers to report for non-drug items and services a numeric count for each of 
those metrics, in addition to the percentages. We support the same requirements for drugs, 
although plan-specific, drug-level reporting would be preferable. Numeric reporting will also 
allow regulators, clinicians and researchers to better evaluate payer practices and identify outlier 
behavior. Further, we recommend that reporting be standardized across health plans.  
We support the addition of the following metrics that are complementary to existing metrics for 
non-drug items and services. All PA metrics that must be reported by impacted payers for 
medical items and services should be extended to drugs.  
â€¢ Total number and percentage of standard PA requests for non-drug items and services 
that remain denied after appeal during the reporting period. 
â€¢ Total number and percentage of expedited PA requests for non-drug items and services 
that remain denied after appeal during the reporting period. 
â€¢ Total number and percentage of standard PA requests for non-drug items and services for 
which the timeframe for review was extended, and the request was denied during the 
reporting period. 
â€¢ Total number and percentage of expedited PA requests for non-drug items and services 
for which the timeframe for review was extended, and the request was denied during the 
reporting period. 
â€¢ Total number and percentage of expedited PA requests for non-drug items and services 
for which the timeframe for review was extended, and the request was approved during 
the reporting period. 
â€¢ Total number and percentage of expedited PA requests for non-drug items and services 
that were approved after appeal during the reporting period. 
For appeals, we support CMSâ€™ proposal to include appeals reviewed internally by the impacted 
payer, as well as by external organizations an impacted payer may contract with to review and 
process appeals. We also support applying all existing and newly proposed reporting metrics to 
PA reporting for drugs.  
Reporting of PA metrics by impacted payers would be significantly strengthened by the 
reporting of all metrics by item and service and stratified by geographic region. This level 
of granularity will allow for more useful and complete information.  
For drugs, transparency would be greatly enhanced by requiring impacted payers to 
publicly report the following PA metrics: 
â€¢ Delineation of all required data by medical and pharmacy benefit. 
â€¢ Delineation by therapeutic category, drug class and indication. 
â€¢ Rates of repeated PA for patients stable on current/maintenance therapy. 
â€¢ Average response times for standard and expedited requests broken down by medical 
items and services, and drugs (broken down by medical and pharmacy benefits). 
STEP THERAPY FOR DRUGS AND BIOLOGICS  
We appreciate that CMS is soliciting public comment on whether increased interoperability of 
information technology (IT) systems across payers could be used to make step therapy and other 
utilization management practices more transparent. This is a worthy endeavor, however, patients 
with GI illnesses need relief now from step-therapy practices. Our organizations implore CMS 
to establish rigorous federal safeguards to protect vulnerable patients from the harmful 
consequences of step therapy, or â€œfail first,â€ insurance mandates. Our experience with the 
suffering of tens of thousands of patients over many years makes clear that technological 
improvements alone will be insufficient to reform the practice of step therapy to the extent 
needed to ensure patients avoid negative consequences. 
Diseases of the gastroenterological tract are complex, chronic, and often progressive conditions 
that â€“ when improperly treated â€” can cause death and disability. Effectively managing these 
diseases often requires pharmacologic or biologic treatment that is driven by a highly 
personalized long-term strategy overseen by a gastroenterologist. When insurers impose step 
therapy, they override doctor-prescribed treatment plans, forcing patients to cycle through 
alternative medications regardless of their clinical need. Absent regulatory oversight, there is 
little incentive for PBMs to preemptively exclude a patient from step therapy when they profit 
from steering patients to ineffective medications. 
Step Therapy Leads to Negative Outcomes 
Far too often, patients are forced to try multiple insurance-preferred medications (multiple 
â€˜stepsâ€™) before obtaining access to the medication that their health care provider originally 
prescribed based on the specifics of their disease status and medical history. For patients with 
digestive diseases, these mandatory delays often carry severe health consequences.  
In IBD, for example, step therapy commonly creates barriers when payers require failure of 
corticosteroids, thiopurines, methotrexate, or a payer-preferred biologic before approving the 
therapy selected by the treating gastroenterologist. This is especially problematic in children 
because treatment selection often depends on severity, growth failure, pubertal delay, extra-
intestinal manifestations, prior infection risk, family logistics, route of administration, 
therapeutic drug monitoring, and the need for rapid steroid-sparing disease control. Common 
examples of step therapy include: 
â€¢ A child with moderate-to-severe Crohnâ€™s disease, growth failure, and elevated 
inflammatory markers is prescribed an anti-TNF therapy or other advanced therapy, but 
the payer requires failure of steroids or immunomodulators first. This is the most 
common scenario that pediatric patients and clinicians encounter. 
â€¢ A patient stable on infliximab after prior loss of response or intolerance to other 
therapies changes insurance and is required to repeat step therapy despite being in 
remission. 
â€¢ A patient stable on vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, adalimumab, or another 
advanced therapy changes insurance and must re-document failure of older therapies 
before continuation is approved. 
The dangers of unmitigated step therapy protocols include: 
â€¢ Irreversible Disease Progression: Step therapy delays access to targeted advanced 
therapies (such as biologics) that are superior in halting disease progression. Active, 
unmitigated digestive disease significantly increases the risk of malnutrition, 
dehydration, developmental delays, strictures, fistulas, bowel perforations, and their 
resulting need for major surgery, and/or hospitalization 
â€¢ Direct Contradiction of Clinical Guidelines: Fail-first protocols directly conflict with 
the Clinical Practice Guidelines for digestive disorders which recommend the early use 
of high-efficacy advanced therapies over step-up approaches to improve long-term 
outcomes and halt disease progression. ,

â€¢ Compounded System Costs: Step therapy fails as a cost-cutting tool. Forcing patients 
to use less safe or ineffective drugs can lead to preventable emergency room visits, 
prolonged hospitalizations, expensive surgeries, and other health complications.

increased health system costs ,  even within the same plan year.

Recommended Federal Protections and Guardrails 
To avoid the dire consequences of unregulated step-therapy protocols, plans should institute a 
standard process that patients and providers can use to request exceptions from step therapy. 
Plans should be required to respond to exception requests within 72 hours of receipt under 
normal circumstances, and within 24 hours in the case of a medical emergency.  
We recommend that patients who meet the following criteria should be exempted from step 
therapy altogether: 
â€¢ The patient already tried and failed on the insurance-preferred drug(s). 
â€¢ Delayed treatment will cause irreversible health consequences. 
â€¢ The insurance-required drug(s) will cause harm to the patient. 
â€¢ The insurance-required drug(s) will prevent a patient from working or fulfilling activities 
of daily living. 
â€¢ The patient is stable on their current medication. 
When a request for a step-therapy exception is denied, payers should be required to include 
patient-specific information detailing the payerâ€™s clinical rationale for denying the request 
(e.g., national medical societyâ€™s guidelines, peer-reviewed clinical literature), the alternative 
treatment covered by the plan, and a description of the right to an appeal. 
We are concerned that many of the insurance programs under CMSâ€™ jurisdiction (e.g., Medicaid, 
CHIP, and the Affordable Care Act (ACA) exchanges) do not regularly offer the standard 
exception process contained in 42 CFR Â§ 423.578 This is the case even though the populations 
covered by Medicaid and CHIP are among the most vulnerable in the nation and are particularly 
susceptible to negative health consequences caused by delayed access to medically necessary 
care. In addition, plans sold on the state ACA exchanges often do not offer an exception process 
at all, and where they do, the process varies widely. This creates a confusing patchwork of

Standardize and Streamline the Step Therapy Exceptions Process  
Currently, there is no standardized approach to applying step-therapy criteria, and payersâ€™ 
methods for obtaining documentation to support a patientâ€™s step therapy history vary widely.  
Typically, under current payer practices, when requesting a waiver or exception to step therapy, 
GI teams typically must submit a letter of medical necessity plus extensive supporting 
documentation and references. This may include diagnosis, disease phenotype, disease severity, 
prior medication history, dates and duration of prior therapies, reason for failure or 
discontinuation, steroid exposure, hospitalization history, lab results, endoscopy reports, 
imaging, growth data, therapeutic drug monitoring, adverse reactions, and prior payer approvals. 
If a patient changes insurance, this process often starts over. Even if the patient is stable on 
current therapy, the new payer may not accept the PA decision, prior step-therapy fulfillment, or 
clinical rationale from the previous payer. The burden then falls on the provider team and family 
to reconstruct records, obtain external documentation, and resubmit information through a new 
portal, fax process, or peer-to-peer review. 
In the end, clinicians bear the brunt of this documentation submission. The American Medical 
Association estimates that physician practices spend, on average, 12 hours per week managing 
the administrative burden associated with insurer-mandated step therapy and prior authorization. 
To ensure the technology solution is designed with both patients and providers in mind, we 
recommend that CMS develop a technology platform to standardize the electronic 
submission of step-therapy information and the exception process across all payers, 
including standard forms and instructions for step-therapy exceptions. 
Payer-to-payer and provider-payer data exchange should include enough information to 
determine whether a patient has already satisfied step therapy or has a clinically justified 
exception. At minimum, this should include: 
â€¢ Current medication, dose, route, duration and target therapeutic level.  
â€¢ Prior therapies tried, with dates and outcomes. 
â€¢ Documented intolerance, contraindication, non-response, loss of response, or adverse 
reaction. 
â€¢ Prior step-therapy exceptions or approvals. 
â€¢ Objective disease activity data, when available. 
â€¢ Treating specialist attestation that the patient is stable and interruption would create 
clinical risk. 
A major pediatric GI issue is that therapies often cross categories. For example, a biologic may 
begin as IV induction under the medical benefit and later transition to subcutaneous maintenance 
under the pharmacy benefit. Similarly, site-of-care mandates may shift an infusion drug between 
hospital outpatient, home infusion, specialty pharmacy, and external infusion center workflows. 
If pharmacy and medical benefit data are not interoperable, the payer may incorrectly 
view the patient as â€œnewâ€ to therapy or lacking documentation, even though the therapy is 
a continuation of established care. In addition, we have all seen cases where IV induction is 
approved and given, only to have the subcutaneous maintenance denied. We strongly 
recommend that step-therapy determinations be transferable across payers and across 
benefit categories. The clinical question should not reset because of the insurance plan, benefit 
type, site of care, or route of administration changes. 
We also recommend that CMS require payers to provide the following information in plain 
language, using a consistent format, to patients and providers: 
â€¢ Patient-specific utilization management requirements, including which treatments, 
services, and prescription drugs have step-therapy requirements, PA requirements, and/or 
formulary restrictions. 
â€¢ Patient-specific cost-sharing information for each treatment, service, and prescription 
drug. 
â€¢ For prescription drugs and services subjected to step therapy, a clear description of the 
exact step-therapy requirement(s) for each applicable service/drug. 
â€¢ Each step-therapy protocol must be based on documented, conclusive clinical evidence 
that the insurance-required medication/treatment is as effective and safe as the initial, 
provider-prescribed medication. 
â€¢ Clear description of the criteria used to determine the appropriateness of a step-therapy 
exception. 
â€¢ Effective dates of step therapy policies. 
It is important to continually evaluate the effectiveness of new policies, systems, and procedures. 
Therefore, we also recommend CMS build future technology systems with public reporting 
in mind. We believe that, at a minimum, there should be publicly available data (as allowed 
under existing patient privacy protections) on the following step-therapy variables: 
â€¢ Total number of step-therapy exception requests. 
â€¢ Medications, diagnostic tests, and/or procedures that are subject to step therapy. 
â€¢ The health indication that the medication/test/procedure is used to treat. 
â€¢ The results of all step-therapy exception requests (approvals, denials). 
â€¢ Reasons for denials. 
â€¢ Total number of denials overturned on appeal. 
Patients Need Continuity of Care Across and Within Plans 
Supporters of step therapy often argue that it prevents medically unnecessary care or direction to 
higher-cost medications when cheaper options suffice.  On the surface, this argument would

hold up most strongly in newly diagnosed patients with no prior treatment history because, in 
theory, a less expensive, straightforward intervention may be sufficient to manage their disease. 
However, research has repeatedly demonstrated that even in these circumstances, step therapy 
often leads to downstream harm (e.g., increased risk of hospitalization) and increased costs that 
could have been prevented by earlier initiation of the originally prescribed medication.

But, the basis for step therapyâ€™s alleged cost savings and prevention of unnecessary care proves 
categorically untrue for patients who have found stability on a medication after insurer-preferred 
medications have failed. Whether the patientâ€™s plan prefers a medication that provides clinical 
stability does not alter the medical reality of patients who have already failed to achieve this 
stability with the options favored by their insurer. In this all-too-frequent instance, there is no 
reasonable clinical evidence to suggest that repeatedly trying the payor-preferred medication will 
ultimately prove successful. Instead, the preponderance of evidence shows that patients who are 
forced to halt an effective treatment experience significant declines in health, leading to higher 
health care utilization (and associated higher costs) and poorer health outcomes.

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Joint digestive disease organizations: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases; American College of Gastroenterology; AGA Institute/American Gastroenterological Association; American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy; Crohn's & Colitis Foundation; Digestive Health Physicians Association; North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association; Advocacy Group
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** National organizations representing digestive disease patients and physicians, including gastroenterology, hepatology, endoscopy, pediatric GI, IBD, liver disease, and digestive health practice leadership.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The joint commenters strongly support expanding electronic prior authorization to all drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits, using HL7 FHIR PA APIs and NCPDP standards, but ask CMS to close operational gaps that affect gastroenterology patients. They recommend stronger interoperability across benefit categories, no duplicative portal documentation, faster and enforceable timeframes, specific clinical denial explanations, granular public PA metrics including AI use, and robust federal step therapy protections, especially for biologics, transplant patients, pediatric GI patients, and patients stable on therapy.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL/RFI on step therapy.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; April 14, 2026 Federal Register proposed rule; 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule; Medicare Advantage step therapy/formulary adequacy concepts.
- **Standards referenced:** HL7 FHIR standards; Prior Authorization API; NCPDP standards for Part D drugs; payer-to-payer and provider-payer data exchange; medical-benefit and pharmacy-benefit standards.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic PA for All Drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** GI drug PA is highly burdensome and often depends on fragmented fax, phone, and portal workflows. Patients with IBD, eosinophilic esophagitis, liver diseases, and related conditions face serious clinical risk from delayed biologics or specialty therapies.
- **Specific request:** Finalize drug ePA requirements and clarify that all utilization management aspects, including site-of-care and dose escalation requests, must be supported through the PA API and transparency requirements.

**Topic 2: Interoperability Across Medical and Pharmacy Benefits**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** Many GI therapies cross benefit categories, such as IV induction under the medical benefit followed by subcutaneous maintenance under the pharmacy benefit. Lack of interoperability can make payers treat continuation therapy as new therapy and create inappropriate denials.
- **Specific request:** Require interoperability between medical- and pharmacy-benefit standards and prevent payers from requiring duplicative proprietary portal documentation when equivalent information has been sent through the standardized API.

**Topic 3: Drug PA Decision Timeframes and Enforcement**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Delays can cause disease worsening, hospitalization, surgery, immunogenicity, graft dysfunction, rejection, and other serious complications. Transplant patients and active GI disease patients need rapid access.
- **Specific request:** Finalize expedited review timelines, adopt the shortest feasible timelines across payer categories, require 24-hour expedited review for liver transplant candidates and recipients, strengthen enforcement, require automatic approval when deadlines are missed, and maintain therapy during appeals or plan transitions.

**Topic 4: Specific Denial Reasons and Specialist Review**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Generic denial language such as failure to meet medical necessity criteria does not identify missing documentation, policy criteria, step requirements, or appeal paths, increasing burden and delaying treatment.
- **Specific request:** Require denial notices to include the specific clinical criterion or policy provision not satisfied, missing documentation, precise payer policy/guideline, step therapy requirement, reviewer qualifications, appeal and peer-to-peer instructions, and review by appropriately qualified specialists.

**Topic 5: Granular PA Transparency and AI Reporting**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Aggregated PA metrics may hide delays or service-specific problems, including high approval rates that mask clinically harmful delays.
- **Specific request:** Require counts and percentages, standardize reporting across plans, report by item/service, geographic region, medical vs pharmacy benefit, therapeutic category, drug class, indication, repeated PA for stable patients, response times, and requests denied or appealed using AI or similar technology.

**Topic 6: Step Therapy and Continuity Protections**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Step therapy can force GI patients to fail less appropriate therapies, contradict clinical guidelines, increase downstream costs, and worsen outcomes. Repeating step therapy after plan changes or formulary changes is especially harmful for patients stable on biologics.
- **Specific request:** Establish federal safeguards, standardize step therapy exceptions, require transferability across payers and benefit categories, prohibit non-medical switching without clinician approval, require continuity of coverage, and require public step therapy reporting.

**Topic 7: Waiver of Step Therapy for Underwater Biologics**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Some physician-administered biosimilars are reimbursed below acquisition cost, making it financially unsustainable for practices to administer them when MA plans require them as fail-first therapies.
- **Specific request:** Establish an MA formulary adequacy standard requiring that any biosimilar in a fail-first position be reasonably available to network providers, or require plans to permit timely access to an alternative biosimilar or reference biologic without additional utilization management.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** The commenters support medical-benefit drug ePA through the PA API and identify technical and workflow challenges involving site-of-care, dose escalation, and biologic documentation.
- **S14:** The commenters support pharmacy-benefit drug ePA using NCPDP standards, while stressing the need for interoperability with medical-benefit data.
- **S15:** The comment directly addresses the medical vs pharmacy distinction and warns that therapies crossing benefit categories must not be treated as new therapy because of benefit or route changes.
- **S16:** The commenters support specific denial reasons and request detailed denial elements including clinical criteria, missing documentation, payer policy citation, step therapy protocols, reviewer qualifications, and appeal instructions.
- **S17:** The request for precise policy criteria, reviewer qualifications, and standardized denial detail implies support for more structured denial communication.
- **S20:** The commenters support CMS's proposed timeframes, urge shortest feasible timelines, and recommend 24-hour expedited review for liver transplant candidates and recipients.
- **S21:** They support implementing ePA for drugs but ask CMS to strengthen enforcement, require automatic approval when deadlines are missed, and maintain continuity during appeals or transitions.
- **S29:** The commenters support PA metrics for drugs and ask for plan-specific, drug-level, service-level, geographic, benefit-level, therapeutic category, class, and indication-level reporting.
- **S30:** They request reporting of PA requests denied and appealed using AI or similar technology.
- **S34:** They support numeric counts in addition to percentages and standardized reporting across health plans.
- **S35:** They support public reporting that lets regulators, clinicians, researchers, and patients identify payer outlier behavior.
- **S66-S82:** The comment responds extensively to the step therapy RFI, requesting standardized exceptions, transferable step therapy determinations, payer-to-payer/provider-payer exchange of treatment history, public step therapy metrics, and continuity protections.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize expansion of electronic PA to drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. Include site-of-care and dose-escalation requests in PA API and transparency requirements.
3. Prohibit duplicative documentation through proprietary portals when equivalent data has been sent through standardized APIs.
4. Require interoperability between medical-benefit and pharmacy-benefit standards.
5. Finalize proposed PA timeframes and adopt the shortest feasible timelines across payer categories.
6. Require 24-hour expedited review for liver transplant candidates and recipients.
7. Strengthen enforcement and require automatic approval when payers miss PA review deadlines.
8. Require continuity of existing therapy during appeals and plan transitions.
9. Require detailed, clinically specific denial notices and qualified specialist review of adverse determinations.
10. Require granular public PA metrics, including counts, percentages, service categories, geography, benefit type, therapeutic category, drug class, indication, response times, repeated PA for stable patients, and AI-related denials/appeals.
11. Establish rigorous federal step therapy safeguards and a standardized exception process.
12. Require step therapy determinations to transfer across payers, plan years, benefit categories, route of administration changes, and site-of-care changes.
13. Prohibit non-medical switching without explicit treating clinician approval.
14. Establish an MA formulary adequacy standard for fail-first biosimilars that are not reasonably available to network providers.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** PA delays for biologics and specialty drugs, inadequate medical/pharmacy benefit interoperability, duplicate documentation, vague denial notices, weak enforcement, opaque PA metrics, AI-related denials, step therapy harms, non-medical switching, and underwater biosimilars.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Increased disease activity, emergency department visits, hospitalizations, surgery, bowel damage, corticosteroid dependence, malnutrition, disease progression, graft dysfunction, organ rejection, immunogenicity, loss of response to biologics, missed school, patient suffering, and higher health system costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Fragmented fax/phone/portal workflows, benefit-category splits, payer data silos, inconsistent step therapy documentation processes, lack of standardized exception forms, annual plan/formulary changes, and financially unavailable fail-first biosimilars.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** AMA estimate that physician practices spend an average of 12 hours per week managing step therapy and PA burden; IBD patient survey result that 85% subjected to step therapy reported negative health outcomes; clinical examples of pediatric Crohn's disease and a 7-year-old with chronic functional constipation forced toward inappropriate alternatives.
- **Studies or research referenced:** National survey on PA burden in gastroenterology; pediatric IBD medication denial article; AMA PA survey; IBD utilization barrier survey; GI clinical guidelines; studies on step therapy costs and harms; research on biologic immunogenicity and anti-drug antibodies; ACP position paper on step therapy and nonmedical switching.
- **Examples provided:** IBD biologics, EoE, liver diseases, IV induction to subcutaneous maintenance transitions, transplant immunosuppressives, anti-infectives, Crohn's disease in children, stable infliximab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, adalimumab, and the Linzess pediatric constipation example.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Digestive disease patients, pediatric patients, transplant candidates and recipients, gastroenterologists, hepatologists, GI practices, payers, PBMs, MA plans, specialty pharmacies, infusion providers, and regulators.
- **Economic implications:** Step therapy and PA delays may increase downstream costs through hospitalizations, emergency care, surgeries, and avoidable complications; underwater biosimilar requirements can impose direct financial losses on physician practices.
- **Technical feasibility:** The commenters support FHIR/NCPDP-based ePA but stress that cross-benefit interoperability, standardized submission, and payer-to-payer/provider-payer data exchange must capture prior therapy and step therapy history.
- **Patient care impact:** Very high; the comment frames timely drug access and continuity as necessary to avoid serious GI disease progression, transplant complications, and loss of response to effective biologic therapy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with strong modification requests
- **Tone:** Professional, clinical, urgent, and evidence-based
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Our societies strongly support CMS' proposal" - Context: Support for expanding PA requirements to drugs under both medical and pharmacy benefits.
2. "Generic denial language is insufficient" - Context: Request for detailed denial notices.
3. "technological improvements alone will be insufficient" - Context: Step therapy RFI response requesting substantive safeguards.
4. "The clinical question should not reset because of the insurance plan, benefit type, site of care, or route of administration changes" - Context: Continuity and transferability of step therapy determinations.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports expedited timelines and asks for enforcement and automatic approval when deadlines are missed.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses administrative burden, downstream utilization costs, and underwater biosimilar reimbursement losses.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Focuses on gastroenterology practice burden from PA, step therapy documentation, portals, peer-to-peer review, and appeals.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Highlights pediatric patients, transplant patients, chronic digestive disease patients, and patients with complex specialty-drug needs.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Supports ePA but identifies cross-benefit interoperability and standardized step therapy data exchange needs.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central concern is timely access to biologics, specialty medications, transplant drugs, and stable maintenance therapy.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Calls for coordination across payers, PBMs, providers, benefit categories, and payer-to-payer/provider-payer exchange.
- [x] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Major focus, especially for therapies moving between IV medical benefit and subcutaneous pharmacy benefit.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests granular PA metrics, AI-related reporting, and detailed denial notices.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Addresses fax, phone, portal workflows, duplicate documentation, formulary changes, and plan transitions.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Standards are referenced but maturity is not the central concern.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Mentions CMS authority for MA formulary adequacy but does not raise legal objections.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed.
